paragraphs: “What are you saying? I’m lost again,” Miüsov broke in. “Another sort of dream. Something shapeless, even impossible to grasp. What is this excommunication? What kind of exclusion? I suspect you’re just amusing yourself, Ivan Fyodorovitch.”

“Yes, but you know, in reality it is so now,” said the elder suddenly, and all turned to him at once. “If it were not for the Church of Christ, there would be nothing to restrain the criminal from doing evil, and no real punishment for it afterward. I mean none but the mechanical punishment spoken of just now, which in most cases only embitters the heart. I mean not the real punishment, the only effective one, the only one that deters and softens, which lies in the conscience’s recognition of sin.”
“How is that, may I ask?” Miüsov asked, with lively curiosity.

“Why,” began the elder, “all these sentences of exile with hard labor, and formerly with flogging as well, reform no one. What is more, they deter hardly a single criminal, and the number of crimes does not diminish but keeps on increasing. You must admit that. So the security of society is not preserved. For although the offending member is mechanically cut off and sent far away out of sight, another criminal always comes at once to take his place, and often two of them. If anything does preserve society, even in our time, and does regenerate and transform the criminal, it is only the law of Christ speaking in his conscience. Only by recognizing his wrongdoing as a son of a Christian society—that is, of the Church—does he recognize his sin against society—that is, against the Church. So it is only against the Church, and not against the State, that the criminal of today can recognize that he has sinned. If society, as a Church, had jurisdiction, then it would know when to call a man back from exclusion and reunite him with itself. But now the Church, having no real jurisdiction but only the power of moral condemnation, holds back of her own accord from actively punishing the criminal. She does not excommunicate him but simply keeps on exhorting him like a mother. What is more, the Church even tries to keep full Christian communion with the criminal. She admits him to church services and to the holy sacrament, gives him alms, and treats him more as a captive than as a convict. And what would become of the criminal, O Lord, if even Christian society—that is, the Church—were to reject him as the civil law rejects him and cuts him off? What would become of him if the Church punished him with her excommunication as a direct consequence of the secular law? There could be no more terrible despair, at least for a Russian criminal, for Russian criminals still have faith. Yet who knows, perhaps then a fearful thing would happen: perhaps the despairing heart of the criminal would lose its faith, and then what would become of him? But the Church, like a tender, loving mother, holds aloof from active punishment herself, since the sinner is already punished too severely by the civil law, and there must be at least someone to have pity on him. Above all, the Church holds aloof because her judgment is the only one that contains the truth, and therefore it cannot, practically or morally, be joined to any other judgment, even as a temporary compromise. She can enter into no agreement about that. The foreign criminal, they say, rarely repents, for the very doctrines of today confirm him in the idea that his crime is not a crime, but only a reaction against an unjustly oppressive force. Society cuts him off completely by a force that triumphs over him mechanically and (so at least they say of themselves in Europe) accompanies this exclusion with hatred, forgetfulness, and the most profound indifference to the ultimate fate of the erring brother. In this way it all takes place without the compassionate intervention of the Church, for in many cases there are no churches there at all. Ecclesiastics and splendid church buildings remain, but the churches themselves long ago strove to pass from Church into State and to disappear in it completely. So it seems, at least, in Lutheran countries. As for Rome, it was proclaimed a State instead of a Church a thousand years ago. And so the criminal is no longer aware of being a member of the Church, and sinks into despair. If he returns to society, it is often with such hatred that society itself instinctively cuts him off. You can judge for yourself how it must end. In many cases it would seem to be the same with us. But the difference is that besides the established law courts we have the Church too, which always keeps up relations with the criminal as a dear and still precious son. And besides that, there is still preserved, though only in thought, the judgment of the Church. Though it no longer exists in practice, it still lives as a dream for the future, and the criminal, no doubt, recognizes it instinctively in his soul. What was said here just now is true too: that if the jurisdiction of the Church were introduced in practice in its full force—that is, if the whole of society were changed into the Church—then not only would the judgment of the Church have an influence on the reformation of the criminal such as it never has now, but possibly the crimes themselves would be incredibly diminished. And there can be no doubt that the Church would look upon the criminal and the crime of the future quite differently in many cases, and would succeed in restoring the excluded, in restraining those who plan evil, and in regenerating the fallen. It is true,” said Father Zossima, with a smile, “Christian society now is not ready, and rests only on some seven righteous men. But as they are never lacking, it will continue unshaken, in expectation of its complete transformation from a society almost heathen in character into a single universal and all-powerful Church. So be it, so be it! Even if at the end of the ages, for it is ordained to come to pass! And there is no need to be troubled about times and seasons, for the secret of the times and seasons is in the wisdom of God, in His foresight and His love. And what in human reckoning seems still far off may by the Divine ordinance be close at hand, on the eve of its appearance. And so be it, so be it!”
“So be it, so be it!” Father Païssy repeated sternly and reverently.
“Strange, extremely strange!” Miüsov declared, with less heat than suppressed indignation.
“What strikes you as so strange?” Father Iosif asked cautiously.

“Why, it’s out of all bounds!” cried Miüsov, suddenly bursting out. “The State is abolished and the Church is raised to the rank of the State. It’s not just Ultramontanism, it’s arch-Ultramontanism! Pope Gregory the Seventh never dreamed of such a thing!”

“You have got it completely wrong,” said Father Païssy sternly. “Understand this: the Church is not to be turned into the State. That is Rome and its dream. That is the devil’s third temptation. It is the other way around. The State is turned into the Church. It will rise and become a Church over the whole world. That is the exact opposite of Ultramontanism and Rome, and of your reading of it. It is simply the glorious destiny ordained for the Orthodox Church. This star will rise in the east!”

Miüsov kept a meaningful silence. His whole figure expressed extraordinary personal dignity. A supercilious, condescending smile played on his lips. Alyosha watched it all with a pounding heart. The whole conversation had stirred him deeply. He glanced casually at Rakitin, who stood motionless at his place by the door, listening and watching intently, though with downcast eyes. From the color in his cheeks, Alyosha guessed that Rakitin was probably no less excited, and he knew what caused his excitement.

“Allow me to tell you a little anecdote, gentlemen,” Miüsov said impressively, with a peculiarly majestic air. “Some years ago, soon after the _coup d’état_ of December, I happened to be calling in Paris on an extremely influential figure in the Government, and at his house I met a very interesting man. He was not exactly a detective, but a sort of superintendent over a whole regiment of political detectives—a rather powerful position in its own way. Curiosity prompted me to seize the chance to talk with him. He had not come as a visitor but as a subordinate bringing a special report, and he saw the reception his chief gave me. So he condescended to speak with some openness—to a certain extent only, of course. He was more courteous than open, as Frenchmen know how to be courteous, especially to a foreigner. But I understood him perfectly. The subject was the socialist revolutionaries, who were being persecuted at that time. I will quote only one most curious remark this man let drop. ‘We are not particularly afraid,’ he said, ‘of all these socialists, anarchists, infidels and revolutionists. We keep watch on them and know all their doings. But there are a few peculiar men among them who believe in God and are Christians, yet are socialists all the same. Those are the people we fear most. They are dreadful people! The socialist who is a Christian is more to be dreaded than a socialist who is an atheist.’ The words struck me at the time, and now they have suddenly come back to me here, gentlemen.”
“You apply them to us, and take us for socialists?” Father Païssy asked bluntly, without beating about the bush.

But before Pyotr Alexandrovitch could think what to answer, the door opened and the long-awaited guest, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, came in. They had in fact given up expecting him, and his sudden appearance caused a moment of surprise.
